passage: Gardeners in one region have noticed that a certain variety of tomato seems to produce more fruit when it is grown near basil plants. In a small experiment, tomato plants grown beside basil yielded about 20 percent more fruit than tomato plants grown alone. These results suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: growing basil near this tomato variety may increase the amount of fruit the tomatoes produce.
basil plants grow larger when they are planted beside tomatoes.
this tomato variety produces more fruit than basil plants do.
tomato plants grown without basil will not produce any fruit.
explanation:
For "most logically completes" questions, the answer should follow directly from what the text just said, without adding anything new.

The experiment showed tomatoes next to basil made about 20 percent more fruit than tomatoes grown alone. The natural conclusion is that basil nearby may boost the tomato harvest.

Choice A says that, and it uses the careful word "may," which fits a small experiment.

rationales.B: The experiment measured the tomatoes' fruit, not how big the basil grew.
rationales.C: The comparison was between two groups of tomatoes, not between tomatoes and basil.
rationales.D: Tomatoes grown alone still made fruit, just about 20 percent less. "Will not produce any" goes much too far.

passage: Archaeologists excavating an ancient settlement found large numbers of fishhooks, fish bones, and stone net weights, but very few tools used for farming. Because the settlement sat on the shore of a large lake, the archaeologists concluded that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the people of the settlement grew most of their own grain.
the lake dried up soon after the settlement was built.
fishing was likely an important source of food for the settlement's residents.
the residents traded their fishhooks to farmers in distant regions.
explanation:
Line up the clues: lots of fishhooks, fish bones and net weights; very few farming tools; and the settlement sits on a big lake.

Every clue points the same way. The people here relied heavily on fishing for food. That's choice C.

A good inference is the conclusion that all the evidence agrees on.

rationales.A: Very few farming tools turned up, which points away from growing most of their own grain.
rationales.B: Nothing suggests the lake dried up. All the fishing gear suggests it was in steady use.
rationales.D: There's no evidence of trade. The fish bones show the residents used the hooks themselves.

passage: Before the invention of photography, painted portraits were the main way for families to preserve images of their members. Portraits, however, were expensive and required many hours of sitting. When photographic portraits became widely available in the mid-1800s, they cost far less and required only a short sitting. As a result, ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: portrait painters began charging more for their work.
many families who could never have afforded a painted portrait were able to obtain images of their members.
families stopped wanting to preserve images of their members.
photographs took longer to produce than painted portraits did.
explanation:
The text sets up a contrast. Painted portraits were expensive and slow. Photographs were cheap and quick.

"As a result" asks what that change led to. If images suddenly cost far less, many more families could afford them, including families who never could have paid for a painting. That's choice B.

When you see "as a result," look for the effect that grows directly out of the cause just described.

rationales.A: The text says nothing about what painters charged after photography arrived.
rationales.C: Cheaper images would make preserving family images easier, not less wanted.
rationales.D: The text says photographs needed only a short sitting, so this contradicts it.

passage: Many species of moth are attracted to artificial lights at night, which can draw them away from the plants they would otherwise pollinate. In a recent study, researchers replaced the white streetlights in one town with amber lights, which moths find far less attractive. Over the following summer, the researchers recorded more moths visiting flowers in fields near the amber lights than in similar fields near white lights in a nearby town. These findings suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: moths are more strongly attracted to amber lights than to white lights.
the amber streetlights made the flowers in the town more fragrant.
moths prefer to pollinate flowers in larger towns.
switching to lights that attract fewer moths may help protect pollination near towns.
explanation:
Follow the chain of reasoning one link at a time.

White lights pull moths away from the plants they pollinate. Amber lights attract moths much less. Near amber lights, more moths visited flowers.

Put together: using lights that attract fewer moths may help keep pollination going near towns. That's choice D.

rationales.A: This is backward. The text says moths find amber lights "far less attractive."
rationales.B: Fragrance is never mentioned. The difference comes from how the lights affect the moths.
rationales.C: The text doesn't compare towns of different sizes.

passage: In the early twentieth century, one city opened a public library branch in each of its neighborhoods. Library records show that branches in neighborhoods with many young children lent far more picture books than other branches did, and over time those branches set aside more shelf space for children's books. This pattern suggests that the branches ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: eventually stopped lending books to adults.
adjusted their collections to fit the needs of the people who used them.
were built only in neighborhoods with many young children.
lent more books overall than the branches in other neighborhoods did.
explanation:
Notice the cause and response. Branches where lots of young children lived lent many more picture books, and over time those branches gave more shelf space to children's books.

In other words, each branch shaped its collection around who was actually using it. That's choice B.

rationales.A: Adding space for children's books doesn't mean adults were turned away. That goes far beyond the evidence.
rationales.C: The text says the city opened a branch in every neighborhood, not only in ones with many children.
rationales.D: The records show these branches lent more picture books, not more books overall.

passage: Art historians sometimes date paintings by examining the pigments they contain. One blue pigment, for example, was not manufactured until the early 1700s. A painting long attributed to an artist who died in 1650 was recently found to contain this pigment throughout its original layers of paint. This discovery suggests that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the painting was probably not made by the artist to whom it has long been attributed.
the artist who died in 1650 invented the blue pigment.
the painting was repaired in the 1700s by a different artist.
blue pigments were widely used by artists before 1650.
explanation:
This works like a time puzzle. The blue pigment didn't exist until the early 1700s. It's found throughout the painting's original paint, so the painting was made after that.

The artist credited with it died in 1650, decades before the pigment existed. So that artist probably didn't paint it. That's choice A.

The phrase "original layers" matters: it rules out the idea that someone added the blue later.

rationales.B: The pigment wasn't made until decades after this artist died, so the artist couldn't have invented it.
rationales.C: A later repair would put the pigment only in the repaired spots. It's throughout the original layers.
rationales.D: The text is about when one particular blue was first made, not how common blue paints were before 1650.

passage: Some plants release chemical signals when insects begin eating their leaves. Researchers found that nearby undamaged plants of the same species increased their production of bitter-tasting defensive compounds shortly after these signals were released. However, when the researchers placed a barrier that blocked airflow between the damaged and undamaged plants, the undamaged plants did not increase their production of the compounds. Taken together, these findings suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: damaged plants produce more defensive compounds than undamaged plants do.
insects avoid plants that release chemical signals.
the barrier caused the undamaged plants to stop producing defensive compounds altogether.
the chemical signals likely reach neighboring plants by traveling through the air.
explanation:
Compare the two setups. With open air between them, the healthy plants responded to the signals. With only the airflow blocked, they didn't respond.

The one thing that changed was the air path, so the signals most likely travel through the air. That's choice D.

This is how experiments reveal causes: change one thing, and see what stops happening.

rationales.A: The study looked at how healthy neighbors responded. It never compares compound levels between damaged and healthy plants.
rationales.B: How insects react to signaling plants is never tested.
rationales.C: The plants didn't increase production, but the text never says they stopped making the compounds entirely.

passage: Historians have long believed that a particular eighteenth-century almanac was printed in only one city, since every surviving copy bears the mark of a printer there. Recently, however, a scholar examined the paper of several copies and found watermarks from two different paper mills, one of which supplied only printers in a distant city. Because printers typically bought paper from nearby mills, the scholar's findings suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: all copies of the almanac were printed in the distant city rather than in the first city.
the printer's mark on the surviving copies was added later by collectors.
some copies of the almanac may have been printed in the distant city, despite bearing the same printer's mark.
the distant paper mill produced lower-quality paper than historians had believed.
explanation:
Here is the reasoning chain. Printers usually bought paper from nearby mills. Some copies use paper from a mill that only supplied printers in a distant city. So those copies were probably printed in that distant city, even though they carry the first city's printer's mark.

Choice C says this and stays careful: "some copies" and "may have been."

On hard inference questions, the right answer often matches the evidence's scope exactly. Watch for choices that say "all" when the evidence only covers "some."

rationales.A: Only one of the two mills connects to the distant city, so the evidence covers some copies, not all.
rationales.B: Nothing suggests the printer's mark was added later. That's a new explanation the text never offers.
rationales.D: The watermarks show where the paper came from. They say nothing about its quality.

passage: A literary scholar notes that the novelist Henrike Vass wrote her first three novels in the first person, each narrated by a young woman recalling her childhood. Her fourth novel, by contrast, moves among the perspectives of six characters of different ages. Several early reviewers criticized the fourth novel as disorganized, but the scholar argues that its structure reflects the novel's central theme: that no single person can fully understand a community's history. If the scholar is correct, then ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: Vass's first three novels were also about the histories of communities.
the shifting perspectives that some reviewers found disorganized were a deliberate choice that serves the novel's theme.
Vass stopped writing in the first person because reviewers had criticized her earlier novels.
the fourth novel is more disorganized than any of Vass's earlier novels.
explanation:
Start from the scholar's argument: the novel's many viewpoints "reflect" its theme that no single person can fully understand a community's history.

If that's right, the shifting viewpoints were intentional and meaningful, not a mess. So what the reviewers called disorganized was really a deliberate choice that serves the theme. That's choice B.

"If the scholar is correct" tells you to accept the scholar's view and follow where it leads.

rationales.A: The first three novels were about narrators remembering their childhoods. Nothing says they were about community histories.
rationales.C: The criticism mentioned was of the fourth novel, which came after the change. It can't explain why she changed.
rationales.D: This sides with the reviewers, which is the view the scholar argues against.
